The Wyoming ground squirrel (Urocitellus elegans) displays a suite of life-history traits typical of hibernating sciurids. At an ambient temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a temperature approximating core body temperature during active euthermic periods, gestational development proceeds relatively rapidly. Field observations indicate that gestation lasts approximately 22.5 days [tg = approximately 22.5 days], a duration that falls within the narrow range of 22 to 23 days reported for this species and aligns closely with values documented in the closely related Richardson's ground squirrel (Urocitellus at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C] richardsonii). This abbreviated gestation period is characteristic of many ground-dwelling squirrels, reflecting an evolutionary trade-off that prioritizes rapid development in seasonal environments where the active season is sharply limited. The timing of parturition is tightly linked to the emergence of spring vegetation, ensuring that neonatal emergence coincides with peak food availability for the lactating female.

Neonates of the Wyoming ground squirrel are altricial and remarkably small at birth, with a typical wet weight of 7 grams [Wwb = 7 grams]. This low birth mass, representing less than three percent of the adult female's mass, is consistent with the pattern observed across the genus Urocitellus, where altricial young are born after a short gestation and undergo most of their somatic growth postnatally. The pups are hairless, blind, and entirely dependent on maternal care during the initial weeks of life. Maternal investment during lactation is substantial, as the female must mobilize stored energy reserves to support the rapid growth of the litter. The neonatal mass of 7 grams provides a baseline from which the subsequent growth trajectory, leading to a much larger adult body size, can be assessed. The success of this early developmental stage is critical for overwinter survival, as pups must achieve sufficient body mass before their first hibernation season.

This variation in weaning age is influenced by litter size, maternal body condition, and local resource abundance in the montane meadows they inhabit. The weaned juveniles must then rapidly acquire foraging skills and accumulate fat reserves before their first winter. Adult body mass, representing the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown individuals, averages around 350 grams [Wwi = around 350 grams] in populations from the central Rocky Mountains. Considerable size variation exists, with published accounts documenting a range from 255 to 396 grams depending on locality, sex, and seasonal fattening cycles.

Sexual maturation in the Wyoming ground squirrel is attained at approximately one year of age, with both sexes reaching puberty at about 365 days after birth [tp = about 365 days after birth] when maintained at a core body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This pattern of first-year maturation is common among small-bodied ground squirrels inhabiting temperate latitudes, where the short active season constrains the time available for growth and reproductive preparation. The timing of puberty onset is critical, as females must emerge from hibernation in the spring with sufficient energy reserves to support both gestation and early lactation. Males typically achieve spermatogenesis before females exhibit their first post-hibernation estrus, a phenological synchrony that ensures reproductive opportunities are maximized during the brief mating window. The age at sexual maturity of 365 days for both sexes represents a life-history strategy that prioritizes early breeding in a seasonal environment where adult survival may be unpredictable.

The maximum lifespan of the Wyoming ground squirrel has been estimated at approximately four years [am = approximately four years], based on data extrapolated from the better-studied Richardson's ground squirrel and limited recapture records for this species at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This longevity estimate, associated with a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C] during the active season, reflects the high mortality rates typical of small ground-dwelling rodents within the family Sciuridae exposed to avian and mammalian predators. In terms of reproductive output, females produce litter sizes ranging from 1 to 11 pups per litter [N_R_i = 1 to 11 pups per litter] and exhibit a reproductive frequency of approximately 6.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 6.5 litters per year], translating to a maximum reproduction rate of approximately 6.5 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 6.5 offspring per year]. This annual reproductive output represents a moderate reproductive rate for a hibernating sciurid, balancing the energetic demands of lactation against the need to accumulate sufficient fat reserves for the subsequent hibernation period.
